steps.title: Choose one glaze route
steps.text: Set out {{ingredients}} and choose one sweetening route before combining. For the mirin version, use the mirin and omit the optional honey and additional soy sauce. For the honey variation, omit mirin and use the measured honey plus additional soy sauce, while retaining the separately listed soy sauce. Do not combine both routes. steps.title: Coat and spread
steps.text: Toss {{ingredients}} with all the chosen glaze in the large bowl. Spread in a single layer, with flat cut faces against the sheet where possible. Keep room between pieces; if the scaled batch piles up, use additional sheets or batches rather than a deeper layer.

steps.title: Watch the coating and centers
steps.text: Roast for 25–30 minutes, gently turning around halfway through and checking the coating then. Test a thick floret with a knife: its center should be tender and the coating browned without blackened bitterness. If the glaze darkens before the centers soften, move pieces away from hot spots, turn the dark faces upward and finish under loose foil while checking the centers; covered pieces will have softer edges. Remove ready pieces promptly rather than requiring every edge to char. More sheet area or larger florets may change the time.

steps.title: Garnish and serve
steps.text: Scatter {{ingredients}} over the hot cauliflower and serve. The sesame seeds and scallions are both included finishes; wash the scallions before slicing and keep them away from raw-meat tools.

changedFields.before:
## Chef's Note

Miso is umami condensed - it transforms mild cauliflower into something deeply savory and addictive. The glaze contains the holy trifecta: miso (salt and depth), mirin (sweetness and shine), and sesame oil (richness). Roasting at high heat caramelizes the glaze onto the florets. This is how Japanese home cooks make vegetables disappear from the plate. The key is not overcrowding the pan; each piece needs direct contact with heat to caramelize.

For a non-vegan variation, replace the mirin with 1 1/2 tbsp honey plus 1/2 tbsp soy sauce, in addition to the separately listed soy sauce. Use mirin for the vegan version.

## Directions

1. **Make Glaze:** In a small bowl, whisk together miso, mirin, soy sauce, sesame oil, rice vinegar, and fresh ginger. Taste - it should taste aggressively salty and umami-rich (the cauliflower will mellow it).
2. **Prep Oven:** Preheat to 425°F. Line a large baking sheet with parchment paper.
3. **Toss:** Pat cauliflower florets dry (moisture prevents caramelization). Place in a large bowl. Pour the miso glaze over and toss with your hands until every floret is coated.
4. **Spread:** Arrange florets in a single layer on the baking sheet, cut-side down. Do not crowd.
5. **Roast:** Bake for 25-30 minutes until the cauliflower is tender inside and the glaze is caramelized and slightly charred on the edges. Shake the pan halfway through.
6. **Finish:** Remove from oven. Garnish generously with sesame seeds and thinly sliced scallions. Serve hot.

## Chef's Note

White miso, mirin, soy sauce, sesame oil and rice vinegar make a concentrated glaze for the cauliflower. This sauce coats the florets before roasting, so check it when turning: miso and sweeteners can darken before a thick center is tender. Split unusually large florets, keep the sheet uncrowded and stop at browned coating and tender centers rather than forcing a black char.

## Directions

1. **Heat and prepare:** Heat the oven to 425°F. Set out a large rimmed sheet or enough sheets for one layer of the measured florets. If lining, use parchment rated for this heat or suitable foil. Wash the cauliflower under running water, divide into similar-sized florets, split very large ones and dry them.
2. **Choose one glaze route:** Set out white miso paste, mirin, soy sauce, sesame oil, rice vinegar, fresh ginger, honey (if using), and additional soy sauce (if using) and choose one sweetening route before combining. For the mirin version, use the mirin and omit the optional honey and additional soy sauce. For the honey variation, omit mirin and use the measured honey plus additional soy sauce, while retaining the separately listed soy sauce. Do not combine both routes. Whisk the chosen ingredients until the miso is evenly dispersed; taste a small sample to understand the salty, sweet and acidic balance.
3. **Coat and spread:** Toss fresh cauliflower florets with all the chosen glaze in the large bowl. Spread in a single layer, with flat cut faces against the sheet where possible. Keep room between pieces; if the scaled batch piles up, use additional sheets or batches rather than a deeper layer.
4. **Watch the coating and centers:** Roast for 25–30 minutes, gently turning around halfway through and checking the coating then. Test a thick floret with a knife: its center should be tender and the coating browned without blackened bitterness. If the glaze darkens before the centers soften, move pieces away from hot spots, turn the dark faces upward and finish under loose foil while checking the centers; covered pieces will have softer edges. Remove ready pieces promptly rather than requiring every edge to char. More sheet area or larger florets may change the time.
5. **Garnish and serve:** Scatter sesame seeds and scallions over the hot cauliflower and serve. The sesame seeds and scallions are both included finishes; wash the scallions before slicing and keep them away from raw-meat tools.

## Honey–Soy Variation

Replace the measured mirin with the measured honey and additional soy sauce from the variation list, keeping the separately listed soy sauce as well. In the original 1½-pound cauliflower batch this is 1½ tablespoons honey plus ½ tablespoon additional soy sauce, giving 1½ tablespoons soy sauce total. Increase or decrease all these amounts with the cauliflower batch; do not add this variation to the mirin route. This honey version is non-vegan. Use mirin and ingredients suitable for a vegan diet for the vegan version.
